ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the University of the West of England College Research Ethics Committee and from Health and Care Research Wales.
table.header: Participants

table.text: This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Approval was granted by the College of Health, Science and Society Research Ethics Committee of the University of the West of England (Ref: HAS.22.08.005) and Health and Care Research Wales (Ref: 24/HCRW/0010).
None of the participants had practical training in interpreting chest radiographs as radiologists but did vary in their exposure to medical imagery (0 to 10 years).
table.header: Participants

table.text: Trainees were recruited via email distributed by the Academy administrative team.
table.header: Participants

table.text: For the pre-and post-assessments participants completed a CXR detection and eye tracking task.
table.header: Stimuli and task

table.text: This task targeted visual detection and localization (distinguishing normal from abnormal) rather than full diagnostic interpretation whereby participants were not required to assign specific diagnostic labels to their findings.
table.header: Stimuli and task

table.text: Participants were seated in front of the monitor and eye tracker, and a verbal explanation of the task was given.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: Participants were instructed to view each image and identify abnormalities as accurately as possible using a mouse click.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: Participants were told that images could contain no abnormalities, a single abnormality, or multiple abnormalities, but they were not made aware of the prevalence of abnormalities across the images (approximately 80%).
table.header: Procedure

table.text: Participants were instructed that there was no time limit but that they should aim to spend no longer than one minute on each image and indicate the end of their search with a spacebar press.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: Before the task began, participants were reminded to maintain a stable viewing distance and minimize head movement.
table.header: Procedure

table.text: Although participants were instructed to avoid head movement as much as possible, inspection of the eye-tracking data during preprocessing indicated a small number of trials were affected by head motion leading to unstable or missing gaze estimates.
table.header: Deviations from preregistration

table.text: Consent to participate: Written informed consent was obtained for all individual participants included in the study.
Consent to publish: All participants provided written informed consent for their data to be reported in aggregate in scientific publications and conference proceedings.

> None of the participants had practical training in interpreting chest radiographs as radiologists but did vary in their exposure to medical imagery (0 to 10 years).

> Trainees were recruited via email distributed by the Academy administrative team.

> For the pre-and post-assessments participants completed a CXR detection and eye tracking task.

> This task targeted visual detection and localization (distinguishing normal from abnormal) rather than full diagnostic interpretation whereby participants were not required to assign specific diagnostic labels to their findings.

> Participants were seated in front of the monitor and eye tracker, and a verbal explanation of the task was given.

> Participants were instructed to view each image and identify abnormalities as accurately as possible using a mouse click.

> Participants were told that images could contain no abnormalities, a single abnormality, or multiple abnormalities, but they were not made aware of the prevalence of abnormalities across the images (approximately 80%).

> Participants were instructed that there was no time limit but that they should aim to spend no longer than one minute on each image and indicate the end of their search with a spacebar press.

> Before the task began, participants were reminded to maintain a stable viewing distance and minimize head movement.

> Although participants were instructed to avoid head movement as much as possible, inspection of the eye-tracking data during preprocessing indicated a small number of trials were affected by head motion leading to unstable or missing gaze estimates.

> Consent to participate: Written informed consent was obtained for all individual participants included in the study.

> Consent to publish: All participants provided written informed consent for their data to be reported in aggregate in scientific publications and conference proceedings.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We aimed to recruit the entire cohort of first-year trainees (N = 15). Based on a previous study using a within-participant design to assess the impact of eye movement modelling training on detecting focal lung pathology in chest X-rays (Brams et al., 2021), we expected medium-to-large effect sizes in comparisons of performance and eye movement measures pre-and post-test. We conducted a priori power analyses using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) to determine an appropriate sample size for detecting effects within the range of Cohen's d = 0.60 to 1.08 at 80% power. Sample sizes ranging from N = 7 to N = 19 are sufficient for this range of effect sizes; therefore, we expected to have adequate statistical power to detect medium-to-large effects with our sample size of approximately 15 participants. However, one trainee was not enrolled on the training course, resulting in a final sample of 14 and effect sizes were smaller than anticipated. Accordingly, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using G*Power (version 3.1.9.4; Faul et al., 2009) to quantify the smallest within-participant effect size that could be detected with this sample size. For a two-tailed paired samples t-test with an alpha level of 0.05 and 80% power, the minimum detectable effect size was dz = 0.81. Thus, the study had sensitivity to detect large within-participant effects but had limited sensitivity for small-to-medium effects.

For a two-tailed paired samples t-test with an alpha level of 0.05 and 80% power, the minimum detectable effect size was dz = 0.81. table.title: Evaluation of an intensive training course on chest x-ray interpretation and competence among trainee radiologists using eye tracking
table.research_questions:
Performance outcomes
The following hypotheses will test differences in performance between session 1 (pre-test) and session 2 (post-test) to evaluate the effectiveness of the training intervention. See Measured Variables for details on measures of performance.
H1: Overall performance outcomes will improve.
H1a: Overall accuracy will be higher in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H1b: The false alarm rate will be lower in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H2: Performance outcomes for single-target trials will improve.
H2a: The accuracy rate for obvious abnormalities will be higher in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H2b: The accuracy rate for subtle abnormalities will be higher in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H2c: The accuracy rate for single-target trials (obvious and subtle abnormalities) will be higher in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H3: Performance outcomes for multiple-target trials will improve.
H3a: The accuracy rate for multiple-target trials will be higher in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H3b: The accuracy rate for subsequent targets after initial target detection will be higher in the post-test compared to the pre-test.

Eye movements
Our hypotheses regarding differences in eye movements pre- and post-test are driven by cross-sectional data that compares the eye movements of radiologists with different levels of training and experience (e.g., resident versus consultant). See Measured Variables for details on measures of eye movements, and how relevant Areas of Interest (AOI) are defined.
H4: Differences in eye movements will be observed pre- and post-test.
H4a: The number of fixations will decrease in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H4b: Fixation durations will be shorter in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H4c: Saccade amplitudes will be larger in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H4d: The time taken to first fixate on an AOI with be shorter in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
H4e: The total time spent in an AOI will increase in the post-test compared to the pre-test.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will use a within-participants design. All recruited trainee radiologists will participate in two sessions, approximately two weeks apart, before (pre-test) and after (post-test) an intensive two-day chest X-ray training course. The two-day training course, led by the National Imaging Academy of Wales (NIAW), aims to help first-year trainees to develop their approach to chest X-ray review and improve pathology detection and clinical interpretation (National Imaging Academy Wales, 2025). 
Participants will complete a visual search task in which they will identify abnormalities within a series of static chest X-ray images. The locations of abnormalities will be identified with a manual mouse click, and trials will be terminated using a space bar press. Stimuli will be presented using MATLAB with Psychophysics Toolbox (Brainard, 1997) whilst participants’ eye movements (see Measured variables) are tracked using Eyelink toolbox (Cornelissen et al., 2002) and the Eyelink portable duo (SR Research). 
There will be two stimulus sets each with 60 images:
•	25 images with subtle* abnormalities (single-target trial)
•	10 images with obvious* abnormalities (single-target trial)
•	15 images with two or more abnormalities (multiple-target trial)
•	10 images with no abnormalities (no-target trial)
The location of each abnormality, if present, will be indicated by a manually defined Area of Interest (AOI) with four co-ordinates (right, left, top, bottom). 
*This set of images were curated by professional radiologists who classified abnormalities on the basis of their visibility and diagnostic clarity.
table.randomization: The stimuli will be presented in a random order. A different bank of images will be used in the pre- and post-test, to control for the possibility of practice effects. These banks will also be counterbalanced across participants, to ensure results are not influenced by potential differences in difficulty between the two chest X-ray image banks.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited through the National Imaging Academy of Wales (NIAW). Participants will be automatically scheduled for a pre- and post-test appointment and will be given the option to opt out from the study without any further notice given. The criteria for inclusion are that participants must be in their first year of radiology training and have a normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Data collection will take place in September 2025, during the weeks immediately before and after the chest X-ray training course.
table.sample_size: We anticipate a sample size of approximately 15 first-year radiologist trainees from the National Imaging Academy Wales (NIAW), the size of the incoming cohort of trainees. We expect to collect data from the majority of trainees based on the automatic scheduling and opt-out model of recruitment.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We are limited to recruiting the full population of radiologists enrolled in their first year at NIAW and completing the chest X-ray training course (N = 15).

We expect medium-to-large effect sizes in comparisons of performance and eye movement measures pre- and post-test based on a previous study using a within-participant design to assess the impact of eye movement modelling training on detecting focal lung pathology in chest X-rays (Brams et al., 2021). We conducted a priori power analyses using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) to determine an appropriate sample size for detecting effects within the range of Cohen’s d = 0.60 to 1.08 at 80% power. Sample sizes ranging from N = 7 to N = 19 are sufficient for this range of effect sizes; therefore, we expect to have adequate statistical power to detect medium-to-large effects with our sample size of approximately 15 participants.
table.measured_variables:
Accuracy and response time	
Performance will be assessed using measures of accuracy focused on the detection of subtle, obvious, and multiple abnormalities. For images containing abnormalities (single- and multiple-target trials), a mouse click within the AOI will be coded as a hit (true positive). A click outside the AOI will be coded as a false positive, and any AOI with no clicks within it will be coded as a miss (false negative). For images containing no abnormalities (no-target trials), any mouse clicks will be coded as false positives. 
Performance outcomes: All trials
1.	Overall accuracy: Percentage of trials completely correct (all targets identified, all non-targets rejected, no false alarms).
2.	False alarm rate: Number of trials with one or more false alarm divided by total number of trials.
Performance outcomes: Single-target trials
3.	Single-target accuracy: Percentage of single-target trials correct.
4.	Obvious abnormality accuracy: Percentage of obvious abnormality single-target trials on which the target was correctly identified.
5.	Subtle abnormality accuracy: Percentage of subtle abnormality single-target trails on which the target was correctly identified. 
Performance outcomes: Multiple-target trials
6.	 Multiple-target accuracy: Percentage of multiple-target trials correct.
7.	 Subsequent-target accuracy: Percentage of additional targets found given an initial target is found.
Performance outcomes: No-target trials
8.	No-target accuracy (correct rejection rate): Percentage of target absent trials correctly rejected (no false alarms).
Response time measures
9.	 Time out rate: Percentage of trials in which the participant timed out.
10.	 Overall response time (RT): Total time (s) from start of trial until the spacebar is pressed to conclude the trial.
11.	 Single-target RT: Total time (s) from start of single-target trial until the spacebar is pressed.
12.	 Obvious abnormality RT: Time taken (s) to click on the obvious abnormality.
13.	 Subtle abnormality RT: Time taken (s) to click on the subtle abnormality target.
14.	 Multiple-target RT: Total time (s) from start of multiple-target trial until the spacebar is pressed.
15.	 No-target (correct rejection) RT: Time taken (s) to conclude (press spacebar) on a target absent trial.

Eye movements
Eye movements will be recorded using the EyeLink Portable Duo (SR Research) at 2000 Hz. Fixation and saccade events will be defined using the default EyeLink parsing thresholds (velocity: 30°/s, acceleration: 8000°/s²). 
The following eye tracking metrics will be calculated across all images, and separately for abnormal and normal images:
1.	Number of fixations: Number of times the eyes remain still.
2.	Fixation duration: Duration (ms) the eye stays still.
3.	Saccade amplitude: Distance (°) travelled by the eye movement.
4.	Saccade duration: Time taken (ms) to make a saccadic eye movement.
5.	Saccade rate: Distance covered (°) per second.
6.	Initiation time: Time taken (ms) to initiate the first eye movement (saccade).
Target-specific eye tracking metrics:
7.	Time to first fixate on abnormality: Time taken (ms) to first fixate on an AOI.
8.	Abnormality visit count: Number of times an AOI is visited before an abnormality is identified.
9.	Dwell time on abnormality: Total time (ms) spent in an AOI.
Categorisation of missed targets:
10.	 Scanning errors: Missed target was never fixated.
11.	 Recognition errors: Missed target was fixated for less than 260 ms.
12.	 Decision-making errors: Missed target was fixated for longer than 260 ms.
table.indices:
Subsequent search misses (SSMs) 
Given the nature of our stimuli, traditional approaches to calculating the SSM effect is not possible. In the current study, there is a significant amount of variance in the number and types of abnormalities (e.g., abnormalities which are more obvious or subtle than others) within multiple-target images, unlike the controlled multiple-target search paradigm which has pre-defined high- and low-salience targets (Adamo et al., 2021). As an approximation of the SSM effect, we will compare subtle single-target accuracy and subsequent-target accuracy.
table.statistical_tests:
Performance outcomes
To test the effectiveness of training on overall performance and performance on multiple-target trials (H1 and H3), we will conduct two-tailed paired samples t-tests between pre- and post-test session. Each relevant dependent variable is listed below:
AH1a: Overall accuracy.
AH1b: False alarm rate.
AH3a: Multiple-target accuracy.
AH3b: Subsequent-target accuracy.
To test the effectiveness of training on single-target accuracy (H2), we will perform a 2 x 2 ANOVA with subtlety (subtle, obvious) and session (pre-test, post-test) as repeated measures factors. 
Eye movements
To examine the impact of training on eye movements (H4), we will perform two-tailed paired samples t-tests between the pre- and post-test session. Each relevant dependent variable is listed below:
AH4a: Number of fixations.
AH4b: Fixation duration.
AH4c: Saccade amplitude.
AH4d: The time taken to first fixate on AOI. 
AH4e: Total time spent in AOI.
Subsequent search misses (SSMs) 
As an estimates of the rate of SSMs, we will compare subtle single-target accuracy and subsequent-target accuracy using a two-tailed paired samples t-test.
Assumption and reliability checks
Equivalence of stimulus banks
To assess the equivalence of difficulty between our set of stimuli, we will conduct a 2 x 2 x 2 ANOVA with subtlety (subtle, obvious), session (pre-test, post-test) and stimulus set (Bank 1, Bank 2) as repeated measures factors.
Test-retest reliability
To examine the test-retest reliability of our measured variables, we will calculate the Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) using a two-way mixed effects model for absolute agreement (Koo & Li, 2016), and Spearman’s Rho. The ICC will take the form:

ICC = [Variance between individuals/(Variance between individuals + Error variance + Variance between sessions)]
table.inference_criteria: We will report frequentist statistics (p-values, alpha = 0.05) and Bayes factors to evaluate the strength of the evidence for the alternative and null hypotheses. Bayesian analyses will be computed using the default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow (JZS) prior with Cauchy distribution (r = 0.707; Rouder et al., 2009) since there is no previous data to guide an informed prior. We will consider BF10 > 6 as evidence for the alternative hypotheses in comparison to the null hypotheses and BF10 < 0.17 as evidence for the null hypotheses in comparison to the alternative hypotheses (e.g., Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2016).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Gaze data will be excluded from analysis when participants are looking outside of the area in which the chest X-ray images are presented. This will be defined as any fixation or saccade with gaze coordinates falling outside the predefined boundaries of the image display window.

We do not plan to exclude any participants on the basis of their performance. First, as trained professionals, we can assume they will engage with the task and provide valid data. Second, there is no clear basis for determining what constitutes valid versus invalid performance with the current stimulus set and task.
table.missing_data_handling: Participants who do not complete the post-testing session will be excluded from any statistical analyses that involve comparisons between sessions.
table.exploratory_analyses:
We do expect that there may be differences in response times from pre- to post-test. Therefore, we will explore differences between our response time measures.  

We will also explore differences in saccade durations, saccade rates and initiation times, and evaluate how search patterns between normal and abnormal images may differ.

AH4e: Total time spent in AOI.
Subsequent search misses (SSMs)
As an estimates of the rate of SSMs, we will compare subtle single-target accuracy and subsequent-target accuracy using a two-tailed paired samples t-test.
Assumption and reliability checks
Equivalence of stimulus banks
To assess the equivalence of difficulty between our set of stimuli, we will conduct a 2 x 2 x 2 ANOVA with subtlety (subtle, obvious), session (pre-test, post-test) and stimulus set (Bank 1, Bank 2) as repeated measures factors.
Test-retest reliability
To examine the test-retest reliability of our measured variables, we will calculate the Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) using a two-way mixed effects model for absolute agreement (Koo & Li, 2016), and Spearman’s Rho. The ICC will take the form:

ICC = [Variance between individuals/(Variance between individuals + Error variance + Variance between sessions)]", "We will report frequentist statistics (p-values, alpha = 0.05) and Bayes factors to evaluate the strength of the evidence for the alternative and null hypotheses. Bayesian analyses will be computed using the default Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow (JZS) prior with Cauchy distribution (r = 0.707; Rouder et al., 2009) since there is no previous data to guide an informed prior. We will consider BF10 > 6 as evidence for the alternative hypotheses in comparison to the null hypotheses and BF10 < 0.17 as evidence for the null hypotheses in comparison to the alternative hypotheses (e.g., Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2016).", "Gaze data will be excluded from analysis when participants are looking outside of the area in which the chest X-ray images are presented. This will be defined as any fixation or saccade with gaze coordinates falling outside the predefined boundaries of the image display window.

We do not plan to exclude any participants on the basis of their performance. First, as trained professionals, we can assume they will engage with the task and provide valid data. Second, there is no clear basis for determining what constitutes valid versus invalid performance with the current stimulus set and task.", "Participants who do not complete the post-testing session will be excluded from any statistical analyses that involve comparisons between sessions.", "We do expect that there may be differences in response times from pre- to post-test. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 4 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of case type (F(1.40, 16.85) = 230.91, p < .001, η²ₚ = 0.95, BF10 = 2.38×10 19 ), as expected, with obvious abnormalities identified more accurately than subtle (t(12) = 25.08, p <.001, d = 6.58, BF10 = 2.06×10 9 ) or multiple abnormalities (t(12) = 20.62, p < .001, d = 6.70, BF10 = 1.00×10 8 ).

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 384 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

ethics_statements: Ethical approval was obtained from the University of the West of England College Research Ethics Committee and from Health and Care Research Wales.
This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Approval was granted by the College of Health, Science and Society Research Ethics Committee of the University of the West of England (Ref: HAS.22.08.005) and Health and Care Research Wales (Ref: 24/HCRW/0010).
live_data_statements: None of the participants had practical training in interpreting chest radiographs as radiologists but did vary in their exposure to medical imagery (0 to 10 years).
Trainees were recruited via email distributed by the Academy administrative team.
For the pre-and post-assessments participants completed a CXR detection and eye tracking task.

This task targeted visual detection and localization (distinguishing normal from abnormal) rather than full diagnostic interpretation whereby participants were not required to assign specific diagnostic labels to their findings.
Participants were seated in front of the monitor and eye tracker, and a verbal explanation of the task was given.
Participants were instructed to view each image and identify abnormalities as accurately as possible using a mouse click.

Participants were told that images could contain no abnormalities, a single abnormality, or multiple abnormalities, but they were not made aware of the prevalence of abnormalities across the images (approximately 80%).
Participants were instructed that there was no time limit but that they should aim to spend no longer than one minute on each image and indicate the end of their search with a spacebar press.
Before the task began, participants were reminded to maintain a stable viewing distance and minimize head movement.

Although participants were instructed to avoid head movement as much as possible, inspection of the eye-tracking data during preprocessing indicated a small number of trials were affected by head motion leading to unstable or missing gaze estimates.
Consent to participate: Written informed consent was obtained for all individual participants included in the study.
Consent to publish: All participants provided written informed consent for their data to be reported in aggregate in scientific publications and conference proceedings.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 10 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:10, File = c("performance_metrics_SA-1.Rmd", 
"AOI_eyetracking.Rmd", "eyetracking_misserrors_KS.Rmd", "eyetracking_misserrors_MP.Rmd", 
"eyetracking_multipletargets.Rmd", "CXR_data_visualisation.Rmd", 
"misserrors_eyetracking.Rmd", "performance_metrics.Rmd", "radiologist_eyetracking.Rmd", 
"radiologist_TPvsTA_NG.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", 
"—", "—", "—", "eyetracking_multipletargets.Rmd", "—", 
"—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "none", "none", "none", 
"none", "dependency", "none", "none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-10L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `CXR_multipletargets_22.04.26.csv` to `Data Files and R Wrangling Scripts/CXR_multipletargets_22.04.26.csv` (in CXR_data_visualisation.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `radiologist_trial_info.csv`, `radiologist_subj_list.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 10 scripts: 6 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Detecting and interpreting abnormalities in chest X-rays (CXR) is a complex visual search task.

Differences between novice and expert performance in medical image perception are well documented but less is known about how early training shapes trainees' detection accuracy, error types, and gaze patterns.
Novices are often taught systematic viewing strategies, yet these may be ineffective without sufficient knowledge of normal variants and pathological appearances.
Educational interventions aim to improve knowledge and recognition of normal and abnormal features, but their impact on scanning behavior and error taxonomy has rarely been examined.
The present study examined the early development of CXR interpretation skills by assessing changes in detection accuracy and visual search behaviour following a two-day training course.
To this end, first-year radiology trainees completed a CXR detection task while their eye movements were recorded before and after training.
Images varied in difficulty, including cases with single obvious or subtle abnormalities and cases with multiple findings.
Trainees showed modest improvements in detecting abnormalities and near-ceiling performance for cases with obvious findings.
However, false-positive rates persisted on over 60% of abnormal cases and over a third of normal cases, and error rates for subtle-and multiple-abnormality cases still exceeded 70% after training.

Most errors arose when trainees fixated abnormalities but did not mark them as abnormal, suggestive of faulty decision-making rather than inadequate scanning or failure to recognize suspicious regions.
These findings suggest that early CXR training should prioritize strengthening discrimination of subtle pathology through perceptual learning and calibration of decision thresholds.
Radiologists are routinely confronted with complex visual search tasks, and successful performance in this context is crucial for diagnosing and staging many diseases (Treviño et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Radiologists are routinely confronted with complex visual search tasks, and successful performance in this context is crucial for diagnosing and staging many diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Treviño et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: At a fundamental level, medical image perception relies on two broad processes: detecting abnormalities through search, recognition and decision-making mechanisms, and interpreting abnormalities using anatomical knowledge among other contextual information (Alexander et al., 2020; Krupinski, 2010).
text.formatted: At a fundamental level, medical image perception relies on two broad processes: detecting abnormalities through search, recognition and decision-making mechanisms, and interpreting abnormalities using anatomical knowledge among other contextual information <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Alexander et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Krupinski, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Worldwide, the most frequently performed imaging examination is the chest X-ray (CXR; Abbott, 2025), which plays a critical role in the early detection of thoracic pathology including lung cancer and pulmonary infections (Agrawal et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Worldwide, the most frequently performed imaging examination is the chest X-ray (CXR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abbott, 2025)</ref>, which plays a critical role in the early detection of thoracic pathology including lung cancer and pulmonary infections <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Agrawal et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the ubiquity of CXR in diagnostic radiology, its interpretation remains prone to missed findings, most of which arise from lapses in the perceptual stages of scanning, recognition, and decision-making (Bruno et al., 2015; Gefter et al., 2023; Kundel, 1989; Lee et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Despite the ubiquity of CXR in diagnostic radiology, its interpretation remains prone to missed findings, most of which arise from lapses in the perceptual stages of scanning, recognition, and decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bruno et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gefter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Kundel, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Lee et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Detecting and identifying abnormalities in CXR is challenging due to the superimposition of several anatomical structures (Gefter & Hatabu, 2023), the presence of "blind spots" (Baker et al., 2013; del Ciello et al., 2017), and the heterogeneity of normal and abnormal lung findings which can also give rise to false positives (Abbott, 2025; Fabre et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Detecting and identifying abnormalities in CXR is challenging due to the superimposition of several anatomical structures <ref type="bibr">(Gefter & Hatabu, 2023)</ref>, the presence of "blind spots" <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Baker et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">del Ciello et al., 2017)</ref>, and the heterogeneity of normal and abnormal lung findings which can also give rise to false positives <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abbott, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Fabre et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: CXR can also contain multiple abnormalities where more salient features naturally attract attention and additional findings can be missed (Berbaum et al., 2015; Samuel et al., 1995), a phenomenon described as "satisfaction of search" (Berbaum et al., 1990 (Berbaum et al., , 1998) ) or the subsequent search miss (SSM) effect (Adamo et al., 2021).
text.formatted: CXR can also contain multiple abnormalities where more salient features naturally attract attention and additional findings can be missed <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Berbaum et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Samuel et al., 1995)</ref>, a phenomenon described as "satisfaction of search" <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Berbaum et al., 1990</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Berbaum et al., , 1998) )</ref> or the subsequent search miss (SSM) effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Adamo et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These challenges are magnified for novices, who might often fail to adopt a comprehensive scanning approach and lack precise anatomical schemas, leaving them vulnerable to missing lesions in visually complex or low-salience regions (Kok et al., 2016; van der Gijp et al., 2014).
text.formatted: These challenges are magnified for novices, who might often fail to adopt a comprehensive scanning approach and lack precise anatomical schemas, leaving them vulnerable to missing lesions in visually complex or low-salience regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kok et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">van der Gijp et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Historically, missed findings in radiology were largely attributed to inadequate visual search.

This view was based on observations that radiologists viewing the same images often utilized highly variable scanning strategies, sometimes leaving regions uninspected (Degnan et al., 2019; Krupinski, 2011).
text.formatted: This view was based on observations that radiologists viewing the same images often utilized highly variable scanning strategies, sometimes leaving regions uninspected <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Degnan et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Krupinski, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In response, "systematic viewing" approaches were introduced, in which anatomical structures are inspected in a fixed order to ensure complete coverage and prevent missed findings (Auffermann et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In response, "systematic viewing" approaches were introduced, in which anatomical structures are inspected in a fixed order to ensure complete coverage and prevent missed findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Auffermann et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Systematic viewing has offered a simple, teachable solution to miss errors and is advocated in many radiology textbooks (Daffner & Hartman, 2013; Eastman et al., 2006; Mettler, 2005), but empirical work provides a more nuanced picture of its effectiveness (Al Elq et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Systematic viewing has offered a simple, teachable solution to miss errors and is advocated in many radiology textbooks <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Daffner & Hartman, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Eastman et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Mettler, 2005)</ref>, but empirical work provides a more nuanced picture of its effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Al Elq et al., 2023</ref>).

text.text: An early observational study showed that a flexible yet complete search pattern achieved better diagnostic performance when interpreting CXR than a rigid but incomplete search pattern (Peterson, 1999).
text.formatted: An early observational study showed that a flexible yet complete search pattern achieved better diagnostic performance when interpreting CXR than a rigid but incomplete search pattern <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Peterson, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Recent eye-tracking studies support this conclusion showing that training students to view images systematically increases systematicity and coverage but does not improve detection of abnormalities compared with non-systematic "look at what draws your attention" instructions (Kok et al., 2016; Van Geel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Recent eye-tracking studies support this conclusion showing that training students to view images systematically increases systematicity and coverage but does not improve detection of abnormalities compared with non-systematic "look at what draws your attention" instructions <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kok et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Van Geel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, experts (radiologists) tend to inspect CXR more systematically than novices (medical students) yet cover less of the image overall (Kok et al., 2016), suggesting that effective expert search involves flexibly prioritizing regions where pathology is more likely (Norman, 2005; Peterson, 1999).
text.formatted: Moreover, experts (radiologists) tend to inspect CXR more systematically than novices (medical students) yet cover less of the image overall <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kok et al., 2016)</ref>, suggesting that effective expert search involves flexibly prioritizing regions where pathology is more likely <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Norman, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Peterson, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Feedback and training focused on where attention is allocated during image perception have been proposed as tools to support search beyond systematic instruction (Xie et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Feedback and training focused on where attention is allocated during image perception have been proposed as tools to support search beyond systematic instruction <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Xie et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Eye movement modelling examples (EMMEs) have long been utilized in areas of psychology to foster enhanced performance and learning (Emhardt et al., 2023; Tunga & Cagiltay, 2023), but only recently have they been applied to medical image training.
text.formatted: Eye movement modelling examples (EMMEs) have long been utilized in areas of psychology to foster enhanced performance and learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Emhardt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Tunga & Cagiltay, 2023)</ref>, but only recently have they been applied to medical image training.

text.text: Early medical image perception studies showed that providing radiologists with feedback on their own eye movement behavior can improve performance (Krupinski et al., 1993; Kundel et al., 1990), an effect that may be strongest early in training (Donovan et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Early medical image perception studies showed that providing radiologists with feedback on their own eye movement behavior can improve performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Krupinski et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Kundel et al., 1990)</ref>, an effect that may be strongest early in training <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Donovan et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Modelling someone else's eye movements when searching for chest pathologies has also been reported to improve visual search and diagnostic decision-making among novices (Litchfield et al., 2010; McLaughlin et al., 2021 McLaughlin et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: Modelling someone else's eye movements when searching for chest pathologies has also been reported to improve visual search and diagnostic decision-making among novices <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Litchfield et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">McLaughlin et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">McLaughlin et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: However, a recent study found that EMMEs did not confer an additional advantage for detecting lung nodules over a control condition with equivalent image exposure and feedback on nodule locations (Brams et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, a recent study found that EMMEs did not confer an additional advantage for detecting lung nodules over a control condition with equivalent image exposure and feedback on nodule locations <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Brams et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although training may guide novices to fixate potential lesion sites, they may lack the conceptual knowledge or templates needed to recognize or correctly interpret what they see (Darici et al., 2023; Norman, 2005; van der Gijp et al., 2014), the latter of which appears to be more effectively developed through intensive, well-structured exposure and feedback to pathology (Brams et al., 2021; Emhardt et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Although training may guide novices to fixate potential lesion sites, they may lack the conceptual knowledge or templates needed to recognize or correctly interpret what they see <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Darici et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Norman, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">van der Gijp et al., 2014)</ref>, the latter of which appears to be more effectively developed through intensive, well-structured exposure and feedback to pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Brams et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Emhardt et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions that teach novices where to look, whether through systematic viewing instructions or EMMEs, have shown limited success.
Together, these bodies of work suggest that training should prioritize radiological content knowledge over prescriptive search patterns (Kramer et al., 2019; Van Geel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Together, these bodies of work suggest that training should prioritize radiological content knowledge over prescriptive search patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kramer et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Van Geel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Eye-tracking studies further indicate that only a minority of misses (30%) reflect pure scanning failures (not fixating an abnormality), and in most cases an abnormality is fixated at least once with errors arising at the recognition or decision-making stages (Kundel et al., 1978).
text.formatted: Eye-tracking studies further indicate that only a minority of misses (30%) reflect pure scanning failures (not fixating an abnormality), and in most cases an abnormality is fixated at least once with errors arising at the recognition or decision-making stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kundel et al., 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, prevailing theories of medical image perception suggest that experts extract a global "gist" that rapidly activates long-term memory representations and guides local inspection to relevant regions (Ericsson & Kintsch, 1995; Haider & Frensch, 1999; Kundel et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Accordingly, prevailing theories of medical image perception suggest that experts extract a global "gist" that rapidly activates long-term memory representations and guides local inspection to relevant regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Ericsson & Kintsch, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Haider & Frensch, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Kundel et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, efficient visual search depends in part on prior knowledge and pattern recognition of normal and abnormal anatomical structures which guide search in a top-down manner (Wolfe et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Within this framework, efficient visual search depends in part on prior knowledge and pattern recognition of normal and abnormal anatomical structures which guide search in a top-down manner <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Wolfe et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This processing style is often operationalized as shorter latencies to fixate abnormalities, longer dwells in relevant regions, fewer overall fixations, and larger saccades, albeit with some variation across case difficulty (see Brams et al., 2019; Brunyé et al., 2019; Gegenfurtner et al., 2011 for reviews).
text.formatted: This processing style is often operationalized as shorter latencies to fixate abnormalities, longer dwells in relevant regions, fewer overall fixations, and larger saccades, albeit with some variation across case difficulty (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Brams et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Brunyé et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gegenfurtner et al., 2011 for reviews)</ref>.

text.text: Findings that repeated exposure to pathology with feedback can induce relatively small but measurable changes in gaze behavior, rather than training of where to look per se (Brams et al., 2021; McLaughlin et al., 2021), are consistent with the idea that the development of target templates is what helps guide attention during image interpretation (Wolfe, 2021).
text.formatted: Findings that repeated exposure to pathology with feedback can induce relatively small but measurable changes in gaze behavior, rather than training of where to look per se <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Brams et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">McLaughlin et al., 2021)</ref>, are consistent with the idea that the development of target templates is what helps guide attention during image interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Wolfe, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The literature reviewed thus far suggests that effective training must enrich trainees' anatomical and pathological knowledge which in turn might strengthen pattern recognition and help guide search during image interpretation.

Consequently, contemporary CXR interpretation course often combine instruction on structured viewing approaches with teaching on normal anatomy, common pathological appearances, and supervised review of clinical cases.
Such interventions may represent a more comprehensive approach to training than programs focused exclusively on search behaviours or viewing strategies.

Course-based interventions that integrate structured approaches to CXR interpretation with teaching and case-based learning have been found to improve students' abilities and confidence in interpreting CXR, although performance generally remains poor for more complex or subtle presentations of disease, particularly when images are assessed without clinical history (Hegazi et al., 2025; Wentzell et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Course-based interventions that integrate structured approaches to CXR interpretation with teaching and case-based learning have been found to improve students' abilities and confidence in interpreting CXR, although performance generally remains poor for more complex or subtle presentations of disease, particularly when images are assessed without clinical history <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Hegazi et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Wentzell et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A common limitation of such interventions, however, is the lack of attention to trainee search patterns, which may reveal the mechanisms through which performance does or does not improve.
There is also an implicit assumption that the majority of false negatives among novices arise because of incomplete visual search, such that lesions are never fixated at all (Krupinski, 2010).
text.formatted: There is also an implicit assumption that the majority of false negatives among novices arise because of incomplete visual search, such that lesions are never fixated at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Krupinski, 2010</ref>).

text.text: Yet we know that omission errors can also arise when abnormalities are fixated but not recognized as abnormal or actively judged to be normal (Kundel, 1989; Kundel et al., 1978).
text.formatted: Yet we know that omission errors can also arise when abnormalities are fixated but not recognized as abnormal or actively judged to be normal <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Kundel, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Kundel et al., 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Many of the studies reviewed here used multiple-target search paradigms where observers were required to detect all clinically relevant abnormalities within a case, closely mirroring real-world practice.

Multiple-target search is especially error prone as detecting one abnormality can impair the detection of additional findings, a phenomenon described in radiology as satisfaction of search (SOS; Berbaum et al., 1990 Berbaum et al., , 1998 Berbaum et al., , 2015;; Kundel et al., 2007; Samuel et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Multiple-target search is especially error prone as detecting one abnormality can impair the detection of additional findings, a phenomenon described in radiology as satisfaction of search (SOS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Berbaum et al., 1990</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Berbaum et al., , 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Berbaum et al., , 2015;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Kundel et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Samuel et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: SOS was originally attributed to premature termination of search due to psychological satisfaction with the image after finding a first abnormality (Smith, 1967; Tuddenham, 1962), but modern empirical work suggests this account is incomplete.
text.formatted: SOS was originally attributed to premature termination of search due to psychological satisfaction with the image after finding a first abnormality <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Smith, 1967;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Tuddenham, 1962)</ref>, but modern empirical work suggests this account is incomplete.

text.text: In most cases, radiologists do continue to search; however, the initial abnormality may bias attention toward perceptually similar findings, leading to misses of dissimilar ones (Berbaum et al., 1990 (Berbaum et al., , 1991)), and/or it may reduce the cognitive resources available to detect additional targets (Berbaum et al., 1991; Cain & Mitroff, 2012).
text.formatted: In most cases, radiologists do continue to search; however, the initial abnormality may bias attention toward perceptually similar findings, leading to misses of dissimilar ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Berbaum et al., 1990</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Berbaum et al., , 1991))</ref>, and/or it may reduce the cognitive resources available to detect additional targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Berbaum et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Cain & Mitroff, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: To capture these multi-dimensional causes, SOS is now commonly referred to as the subsequent search miss effect (SSM; Adamo et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To capture these multi-dimensional causes, SOS is now commonly referred to as the subsequent search miss effect (SSM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Adamo et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, only one CXR study has explicitly applied this error taxonomy to SSM errors and compared the pattern of misses in single-versus multiple-target search showing that 90% of subsequent missed abnormalities were fixated (Samuel et al., 1995).
text.formatted: To our knowledge, only one CXR study has explicitly applied this error taxonomy to SSM errors and compared the pattern of misses in single-versus multiple-target search showing that 90% of subsequent missed abnormalities were fixated <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Samuel et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: This is in direct contrast with work using simplified multiple-target search displays that suggest that over half of SSM errors originate from incomplete scanning (Birch-Hurst et al., in preparation; Cain et al., 2013), although this is likely because locations of abnormalities in CXR are somewhat predictable (Adamo et al., 2021).

text.text: Understanding how CXR interpretation education shapes both diagnostic performance and visual search during the earliest phase of radiology training is crucial, yet empirical evidence in this group is sparse.

Existing work on systematic viewing, EMMEs, and content-focused courses has largely examined mixed cohorts of medical students and more advanced trainees, reported only global accuracy indices, or omitted detailed eye-tracking and error taxonomies.

Moreover, abnormalities in CXR vary widely in location, salience, and conspicuity, and few studies have considered how training influences the localization of abnormalities across the full range of radiographic presentations.

The present study therefore focuses specifically on first-year radiology trainees, who are expected to already be familiar with normal anatomy and common chest pathology but are still developing specialized interpretative skills.

Addressing these gaps is theoretically important because visual search expertise, perceptual expertise and diagnostic expertise may develop at different rates (Kelly et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Addressing these gaps is theoretically important because visual search expertise, perceptual expertise and diagnostic expertise may develop at different rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Kelly et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Waite et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Examining both gaze behaviour and performance outcomes can therefore distinguish whether early education is associated with changes in search, abnormality detection, or the relationship between these processes.
Our first aim was to examine whether trainees' ability to detect and localize abnormalities changed following participation in a two-day, structured CXR course.

The CXR training course integrated guidance on search approaches with teaching of chest anatomical and pathological features through case-based learning, and performance was accordingly assessed across cases that varied in their complexity/difficulty (e.g., cases with subtle abnormalities, obvious abnormalities and multiple abnormalities).

Building on work showing that expert search is characterised by selective attention to task-relevant regions and more efficient global-local processing, our second aim investigated whether trainees' search patterns changed in an expert-like direction following brief training (e.g., fewer fixations, shorter average fixation durations, shorter latencies to first fixate on abnormalities, longer dwell times on abnormalities, and larger saccade amplitudes).

Our third aim was to characterize the taxonomy of trainee miss errors (scanning, recognition, and decisionmaking) and to assess changes in the frequency and relative prevalence of these error types following training, thereby providing insight into the processes underlying changes in detection performance and visual search behaviour.
The study was preregistered at the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to data collection.
The preregistered protocol, including the planned hypotheses, methods, and analysis plan is available at https://osf.io/mutq3/overview.

text.text: Fourteen trainee radiologists (5 women, 9 men, Mage = 29.07, SD = 1.86) from the National Imaging Academy of Wales took part in the study.

To be eligible to take part, participants needed to be in their first year of radiological training and enrolled on the twoday chest radiograph interpretation course taking place at the Academy campus.
None of the participants had practical training in interpreting chest radiographs as radiologists but did vary in their exposure to medical imagery (0 to 10 years).
Trainees were recruited via email distributed by the Academy administrative team.
The voluntary nature of the study was stated and confirmation of participation with a scheduled appointment was obtained prior to collecting written informed consent.
Ethical approval was obtained from the University of the West of England College Research Ethics Committee and from Health and Care Research Wales.
We aimed to recruit the entire cohort of first-year trainees (N = 15).

Based on a previous study using a within-participant design to assess the impact of eye movement modelling training on detecting focal lung pathology in chest X-rays (Brams et al., 2021), we expected medium-to-large effect sizes in comparisons of performance and eye movement measures pre-and post-test.
text.formatted: Based on a previous study using a within-participant design to assess the impact of eye movement modelling training on detecting focal lung pathology in chest X-rays <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Brams et al., 2021)</ref>, we expected medium-to-large effect sizes in comparisons of performance and eye movement measures pre-and post-test.

text.text: We conducted a priori power analyses using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) to determine an appropriate sample size for detecting effects within the range of Cohen's d = 0.60 to 1.08 at 80% power.
text.formatted: We conducted a priori power analyses using G*Power 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Faul et al., 2009)</ref> to determine an appropriate sample size for detecting effects within the range of Cohen's d = 0.60 to 1.08 at 80% power.

text.text: Sample sizes ranging from N = 7 to N = 19 are sufficient for this range of effect sizes; therefore, we expected to have adequate statistical power to detect medium-to-large effects with our sample size of approximately 15 participants.
However, one trainee was not enrolled on the training course, resulting in a final sample of 14 and effect sizes were smaller than anticipated.

Accordingly, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using G*Power (version 3.1.9.4; Faul et al., 2009) to quantify the smallest within-participant effect size that could be detected with this sample size.
text.formatted: Accordingly, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using G*Power (version 3.1.9.4; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Faul et al., 2009)</ref> to quantify the smallest within-participant effect size that could be detected with this sample size.

text.text: For a two-tailed paired samples t-test with an alpha level of 0.05 and 80% power, the minimum detectable effect size was dz = 0.81.
Thus, the study had sensitivity to detect large within-participant effects but had limited sensitivity for small-to-medium effects.
The study employed a pre-versus post-experimental design with a single group of trainees and was conducted in three phases.
The first phase involved a pre-intervention assessment of accuracy at detecting CXR abnormalities and scan path behavior, plus a short demographic questionnaire.
During the second phase, trainees completed a two-day CXR interpretation course designed to improve search patterns and anatomical/diagnostic knowledge.
The first day comprised of online lecture content on chest imaging techniques and image quality assessment, CXR anatomy and normal variants, and approaches to interpreting and reporting CXR.

The second day involved rotating through case-based review sessions on lung pathology, pleural/hilar/mediastinal pathology, cardiovascular disease and key review areas, medical artefacts (e.g., lines, tubes, devices), and chest wall and upper abdominal pathology.
The final phase involved a post-intervention assessment using the same task as in the first phase but with a different set of CXR images.
For the pre-and post-assessments participants completed a CXR detection and eye tracking task.
In each testing session, participants viewed several posterior-anterior static radiographs presented in a random order and were instructed to decide on the presence and location of any abnormalities.

This task targeted visual detection and localization (distinguishing normal from abnormal) rather than full diagnostic interpretation whereby participants were not required to assign specific diagnostic labels to their findings.
Images presented without any clinical history as previous work has shown that clinical information can influence viewing behavior (Kundel & Wright, 1969).
text.formatted: Images presented without any clinical history as previous work has shown that clinical information can influence viewing behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Kundel & Wright, 1969)</ref>.

text.text: Since our primary interest was in how training altered scanning patterns and abnormality detection rather than high-level interpretive processes (e.g., mapping findings onto diagnoses and management decisions), we sought to minimize the influence of contextual factors such as clinical history.
For the task, two image banks were created and analyzed by a consulting radiologist specializing in thoracic imaging.
Images which were poor quality, unclear, or were unable to be deidentified were not included.

The final image banks contained 60 chest radiographs, and these banks (A and B) were counterbalanced such that half of the participants viewed bank A in the pre-test and bank B in the post-test, while the other half viewed the banks in the reverse order to minimize practice effects.
Each image bank included chest radiographs that were normal or contained one or more abnormalities.

Within a single bank, 25 images contained a single subtle abnormality, 10 contained a single obvious abnormality, 15 contained multiple abnormalities varying in subtlety and number, and 10 contained no abnormalities (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Within a single bank, 25 images contained a single subtle abnormality, 10 contained a single obvious abnormality, 15 contained multiple abnormalities varying in subtlety and number, and 10 contained no abnormalities (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Images varied in size and subtended areas from 31.0 × 38.5 degrees of visual angle (°) to 56.9°× 50.1°.
Example Chest Radiograph Images Note.
Sample chest radiographs for the detection and eye-tracking task.
The right side of the images correspond to the left side of the body.

Images contained (A) a single subtle abnormality (right upper zone lesion), (B) no abnormalities (normal), (C) a single obvious abnormality (left upper zone mass), and (D) multiple abnormalities (right middle zone lesion and right pneumothorax).

A B were manifestations of various diseases including adenocarcinoma, metastasis, sarcoidosis, chronic lung allograft dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, and tuberculosis.
Abnormalities were defined within an area of interest (AOI) using EyeLink Data Viewer.
Axis-aligned rectangular regions were drawn manually around each abnormality within an image.
Each AOI was specified in screen-pixel coordinates by its left, top, right, and bottom boundaries.

Pixels areas covered by each AOI varied across images, reflecting differences in lesion size and spatial extent (e.g., more diffuse abnormalities such as lobar atelectasis or extensive consolidation were enclosed in larger rectangles).

Stimuli were presented on a 21.5" Dell P2217H LCD monitor (brightness 250 cd/m 2 ) with a 1920 × 1200 resolution and 60 Hz refresh rate using MATLAB with Psychophysics toolbox (Brainard, 1997) at a viewing distance of approximately 80 cm.
text.formatted: Stimuli were presented on a 21.5" Dell P2217H LCD monitor (brightness 250 cd/m 2 ) with a 1920 × 1200 resolution and 60 Hz refresh rate using MATLAB with Psychophysics toolbox <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Brainard, 1997)</ref> at a viewing distance of approximately 80 cm.

text.text: Eye movements were tracked monocularly using the Eyelink Portable Duo (SR Research) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz in a remote unrestrained mode.

The eye tracker was mounted on a tripod and placed approximately 55 cm from the participant's eyes and was controlled with the Eyelink Host PC (Dell Latitude 5420 Core i5 11 th Gen) and Eyelink toolbox in MATLAB (Cornelissen et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The eye tracker was mounted on a tripod and placed approximately 55 cm from the participant's eyes and was controlled with the Eyelink Host PC (Dell Latitude 5420 Core i5 11 th Gen) and Eyelink toolbox in MATLAB <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Cornelissen et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Pre-and post-testing data was collected on the Academy campus in a low-lit room that resembled a typical reporting environment.
Participants were seated in front of the monitor and eye tracker, and a verbal explanation of the task was given.
Participants were instructed to view each image and identify abnormalities as accurately as possible using a mouse click.

Participants were told that images could contain no abnormalities, a single abnormality, or multiple abnormalities, but they were not made aware of the prevalence of abnormalities across the images (approximately 80%).
Participants were instructed that there was no time limit but that they should aim to spend no longer than one minute on each image and indicate the end of their search with a spacebar press.
A target sticker was placed on the forehead above the eyebrow of the tracked eye to enable head position tracking.
This was followed by a standard 9-point calibration procedure.
The calibration was accepted if the average error was below 0.5° and the maximum error was no larger than 1.2°.
Before the task began, participants were reminded to maintain a stable viewing distance and minimize head movement.
Between each trial a fixation cross appeared in the center of the screen.
Participants confirmed their fixation and readiness to proceed to the next trial by pressing the spacebar.
If a spatial mismatch between the recorded and actual gaze positions was observed between trials, a drift correction was applied.
The task took approximately 45 minutes to complete in total.
In the pre-test session, the task was followed by a brief demographic questionnaire.
Approximately one week later, participants attended the two-day CXR interpretation course.
Upon completing the course, they returned for the post-test session, which followed the same procedure as the pre-test using the alternative image bank.
Planned measurements, data exclusions and analyses deviated from the preregistration in the following ways: 1.
We initially planned to assess accuracy for abnormal cases as the proportion of images where all abnormalities were identified and no false positive identifications were made.
In practice, participants showed a high false alarm rate meaning very few trials met this criterion.
To obtain more informative indices of performance we instead considered cases to be accurate if all abnormalities had been correctly identified irrespective of any additional false positive marks.

We planned to categorize misses into scanning, recognition, and decision-making errors using a 260 millisecond (ms) fixation duration threshold, based on work using a simplified multiple-target search task (Cain et al., 2013).
text.formatted: We planned to categorize misses into scanning, recognition, and decision-making errors using a 260 millisecond (ms) fixation duration threshold, based on work using a simplified multiple-target search task <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Cain et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, the radiology literature suggests this value is not appropriate for our CXR stimuli, where recognition of abnormalities require longer dwell times.
We therefore revised the threshold to a dwell time of 600 ms in line with the error taxonomy of prior work in radiology (Kundel et al., 1978).
text.formatted: We therefore revised the threshold to a dwell time of 600 ms in line with the error taxonomy of prior work in radiology <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kundel et al., 1978)</ref>.

text.text: There were a few instances in which participants expressed to the researcher that they had accidentally terminated the trial before they had finished searching, and these trials were removed from all performance and eye movement analyses since they did not reflect valid performance (n = 4).

Although participants were instructed to avoid head movement as much as possible, inspection of the eye-tracking data during preprocessing indicated a small number of trials were affected by head motion leading to unstable or missing gaze estimates.

To identify trials with unstable tracking, we examined the mean saccade duration per trial; trials with an average saccade duration exceeding 200 ms were taken to reflect pronounced tracking drift and were excluded from all eye movement analyses.
This criterion was applied uniformly across participants and sessions and resulted in the removal of only a small proportion of trials overall (<1%).
text.formatted: This criterion was applied uniformly across participants and sessions and resulted in the removal of only a small proportion of trials overall (<1%).

text.text: We originally planned to conduct a 2 × 2 repeated measures ANOVA with session (pre, post) and subtlety (subtle, obvious) as within-participant factors.
However, subtle, obvious and multiple-target images each represent three distinct levels of difficulty and diagnostic complexity in our stimulus set.

Since training effects might reasonably differ across the full range of abnormal cases, we revised the subtlety factor to case type (subtle, obvious, multiple), resulting in a 2 × 3 repeated measures ANOVA.
To assess the impact of training, we calculated several performance measures within the pre-and post-test data.
For abnormal cases, accurate detection was defined as correctly identifying all abnormalities present (single subtle, single obvious, multiple) irrespective of any additional false positive markings.

Accuracy rates for abnormal images were therefore calculated as the proportion of correct cases divided by total number of cases for each case type separately (subtle accuracy, obvious accuracy, multiple-target accuracy).
As an additional index of multiple-target accuracy, we calculated subsequent-target accuracy (proportion of additional abnormalities detected given at least one abnormality had been found).

The correct rejection rate was calculated as the proportion of images correctly identified as normal with no false positives, and the proportion of abnormal images with at least one false positive reflected the false alarm rate.
Total search time was measured as the time elapsed between stimulus onset and trial termination (spacebar press) in seconds (s).
To examine search behavior, we extracted several eye-movement metrics within each testing phase.
Fixation and saccadic events were classified using EyeLink's default velocity
All missed abnormalities across all abnormal images were categorized according to the fixation data (Carmody et al., 1980; Kundel et al., 1978; Samuel et al., 1995).
text.formatted: All missed abnormalities across all abnormal images were categorized according to the fixation data <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Carmody et al., 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Kundel et al., 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Samuel et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: If an abnormality was never fixated, it was classified as a scanning error.
If an abnormality was fixated but the total dwell time was less than 600 ms, it was categorized as a recognition error.
Missed abnormalities with dwell times more than 600 ms were classified as decisionmaking errors.
We calculated the counts of each error type across the pre-and post-test sessions as well as their proportions.
We report both traditional frequentist statistics using p-values and Bayesian statistics using Bayes factors.
Frequentist significance was assessed using an alpha level of .05.
To evaluate the strength of the evidence, Bayes factors were computed using the Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow (JZS) prior (r = .707; Rouder et al., 2009) in JASP (JASP Team, 2025).
text.formatted: To evaluate the strength of the evidence, Bayes factors were computed using the Jeffreys-Zellner-Siow (JZS) prior (r = .707; <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Rouder et al., 2009)</ref> in JASP (JASP Team, 2025).

text.text: Accordingly, a BF10 > 6 was considered evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis over the null, whereas a BF10 < .17 was interpreted as evidence in favor of the null hypothesis over the alternative hypothesis (Wagenmakers et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Accordingly, a BF10 > 6 was considered evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis over the null, whereas a BF10 < .17 was interpreted as evidence in favor of the null hypothesis over the alternative hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Wagenmakers et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For our inferential statistics, where relevant, tests of sphericity were carried out using Mauchly's test.
In cases where sphericity was violated, we report the Greenhouse-Geisser-corrected degrees of freedom and p-values.

Before examining training effects, we assessed whether the two stimulus banks differed in difficulty across abnormal image types at baseline using a mixed 2 x 3 ANOVA with stimulus bank (A, B) as a between-participant factor and case type (subtle, obvious, multiple) as a within-participant factor.

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of case type (F(1.40, 16.85) = 230.91, p < .001, η²ₚ = 0.95, BF10 = 2.38×10 19 ), as expected, with obvious abnormalities identified more accurately than subtle (t(12) = 25.08, p <.001, d = 6.58, BF10 = 2.06×10 9 ) or multiple abnormalities (t(12) = 20.62, p < .001, d = 6.70, BF10 = 1.00×10 8 ).
text.formatted: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of case type (F(1.40, 16.85) = 230.91, p < .001, η²ₚ = 0.95, BF10 = 2.38×10 19 ), as expected, with obvious abnormalities identified more accurately than subtle (t(12) = 25.08, p <.001, d = 6.58, BF10 = 2.06×10 9 ) or multiple abnormalities (t(12) = 20.62, p < .001, d = 6.70, BF10 = 1.00×10 8 ).

text.text: There was no significant main effect of stimulus bank (F(1, 12) = 1.92, p = 0.191, η²ₚ = 0.14, BF10 = 0.38) and no significant stimulus bank × trial type interaction (F(1.40, 16.85) = 1.39, p = 0.267, η²ₚ = 0.10, BF10 = 0.62), indicating no evidence that the two image banks differed at baseline.

Differences in detection accuracy for subtle, obvious and multiple abnormalities across the pre-and post-testing phases were assessed with a 2 × 3 repeated measures ANOVA with time (pre, post) and case type (subtle, obvious, multiple) as within-participant factors.

The repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of time (F(1, 13) = 5.07, p = .042, η²ₚ = .28, BF10 = 1.71; Figure 2) where accuracy at detecting abnormalities improved post-test relative to pre-test collapsed across case type (t(13) = 2.25, p = .042, d = 0.54, BF10 = 4.86).

text.text: There was also a significant main effect of case type (F(1.31, 16.98) = 474.26, p < .001, η²ₚ = .97, BF10 = 2.45×10 18 ), where accuracy at identifying obvious abnormalities was significantly higher than accuracy at identifying subtle abnormalities (t(13) = 32.35, p < .001, d = 6.26, BF10 = 4.17×10 20 ) and all abnormalities in images with multiple targets (t(13) = 34.96, p < .001, d = 6.42, BF10 = 2.16×10 19 ) across both testing phases.

text.text: There were no differences in accuracy between subtle and multiple-target cases collapsed across the pre-and post-test (t(13) = 0.53, p = .526, d = 0.16, BF10 = 0.24) suggesting that initial abnormality detection did not affect subsequent abnormality detection.
The time × case type interaction was not significant (F(2, 26) = 0.18, p = .834, η²ₚ = .01, BF10 = 0.21).

Despite small improvements in detection accuracy, the false alarm rate across abnormal images was consistent across both testing phases (t(13) = 0.33, p = .751, d = 0.09, BF10 = 0.28; Table 1), and the tendency to report false positive findings in normal images also remained consistent as reflected in the correct rejection rate (t(13) = 1.17, p = .265, d = 0.31, BF10 = 0.48).

text.text: Further paired samples t-tests did not indicate significant changes in the proportion of additional abnormalities found after an initial abnormal finding was identified (t(13) = 0.43, p = .677, d = 0.11, BF10 = 0.29) from pre-to post-test.
The total time searching each image also did not change significantly from pre-to post-test (t(13) = 1.06, p = .307, d = 0.28, BF10 = 0.44).

Table 2 reports the descriptive statistics for our eye movement measures before and 492 after training.
To assess the impact of training on our primary eye movement measures, we 493 performed one-tailed paired samples t-tests across the pre-and post-test phases.

There were 494 no significant changes in fixation counts (t(13) = 1.40, p = .093, d = 0.38, BF+0 = 1.08), time 495 to first fixate on an abnormality (t(13) = 0.58, p = .287, d = 0.15, BF+0 = 0.44), fixation 496 durations (t(13) = 1.56, p = .929, d = 0.42, BF+0 = 0.12), saccade amplitudes (t(13) = 1.58, p497 = .931, d = 0.42, BF-0 = 0.12), or the dwell time on an abnormality (t(13) = 0.60, p = .720, d = 498 0.16, BF-0 = 0.18).

Two-tailed paired samples t-tests across the pre-and post-test phases also 499 revealed no significant changes in the saccade rate (t(13) = 1.27, p = .228, d = 0.34, BF10 = 500 0.53), saccade duration (t(13) = 0.85, p = .411, d = 0.23, BF10 = 0.37), or the time to first 501 initiate an eye movement (t(13) = 0.80, p = .437, d = 0.22, BF10 = 0.36).
Although there were small improvements in accuracy overall, miss errors remained 507 prevalent (see Figure 3).
